subject: Post-demo: Connection design + streaming latency constraints
messages:
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
To: Amira Khan <amira@brightlane.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 05 Oct 2028 14:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: Connection design + streaming latency constraints

Hi Amira — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick recap from our call and a proposed set of next steps so we can align on SLOs and the rate/quota approach.

Key requirements you shared:
- Peak concurrent streaming sessions: ~150 (live transcripts + summarization).
- Typical sustained throughput: ~30–45 requests/sec outside peak windows.
- Bursts: up to 300 concurrent short-lived calls during business events (1–3 minutes).
- Streaming latency: first-byte streaming target <250ms for 95th percentile; per-token emission target ~<200ms.
- Connection model: prefer long-lived connection pooling from edge (client keeps 4–8 TCP/TLS connections to Redwood SDK) with per-connection multiplexing if possible.
- Token characteristics: average response length ~120–300 tokens, many short-turn streams.

Questions we need clarified from your side before we issue a formal quota/price proposal:
1) Average session duration during peak (minutes).
2) Percent of requests that use streaming vs non-streaming (rough estimate).
3) Any regulatory/retention constraints that would require Private deployment instead of Hosted.

Next steps (proposed):
- Redwood to follow up with a rate/quota proposal (sustained QPS, burst limits, recommended per-connection multiplexing) and a ballpark price for a Dedicated pool vs Hosted with burst capacity.
- Schedule a technical deep dive with our infra team next week to walk through connection pooling and streaming tests (we’ll bring an infra engineer).
- Amira/procurement to share expected procurement timeline and PO requirements.

Attaching: slo_requirements_Amira.xlsx (high-level traffic profile you shared).

Thanks — I’ll draft a short options doc after the infra sync and include a simple canary plan for initial rollout.

—Lauren

Thanks Lauren — that matches my notes. A few clarifications:
- Average session during peaks is ~7–12 minutes (most live sessions close in ~10m).
- Streaming vs non-streaming mix: roughly 70% streaming, 30% normal request/response.
- Bursts happen 2–3 times per week (scheduled campaigns) and can push median active sessions from 80 to ~250 for 2–5 minutes.
- For compliance: we are HIPAA-adjacent; retention policy is strict but we can start on Hosted if data-in-transit & KMS meet requirements. Private/on-prem is possible but procurement prefers Hosted + contractual controls initially.

Procurement timeline: we’re aiming to get vendor T&Cs and budget approval by end of month. I’ll loop in legal if we progress.

Can you give a high-level on how Redwood counts concurrency vs QPS? Are connection multiplexing channels counted as separate concurrent sessions? That’s a critical piece for our capacity planning.

—Amira
Director of Product, Brightlane Health
amira@brightlane.com
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>

Looping in a slightly more prescriptive response so we can get a quick parity check from product/infra. High level answers to Amira’s question and an initial plan: 

How Redwood counts resources (high level):
- Concurrency: we count active model sessions (a session is an in-flight streaming or non-streaming request that is holding compute). If a single long-lived connection multiplexes N independent streams, each independent in-flight stream counts as one concurrent session.
- Connections: TCP/TLS connections are a transport concern; we encourage connection pooling to reduce handshake overhead, but we enforce concurrency and QPS limits at the session/request level.
- QPS/Rate limits: we apply per-API-key sustained QPS and a burst ceiling. The burst ceiling accommodates short spikes but is time-windowed (e.g., 1 minute rolling).

Initial sizing guidance (ballpark for your profile):
- To cover steady-state + frequent bursts: reserve capacity for ~250 concurrent sessions (covers scheduled campaigns and headroom).
- Sustained API QPS: recommend a committed baseline of 120 QPS with a burst window up to 350 QPS for 1–5 minute events.
- Streaming concurrency: for 150 concurrent streams at ~10 tokens/sec average, plan for ~1.5k tokens/sec aggregate; ensure KV/prefix cache is enabled for repeated prompt patterns to reduce cost.

Options we can quote: 
1) Hosted w/ burst credits: no upfront infra commitment; committed baseline (120 QPS), burst pool for events, and a per-token rate for overages. Good for faster procurement.
2) Dedicated pool (recommended for strict SLOs): dedicated GPUs sized to meet 250 concurrent sessions with guaranteed throughput and lower tail latency. Includes SLA and can be integrated with your KMS.

For next steps I’ll ask Infra to confirm exact GPU sizing (we typically model with our internal perf profiles) and produce a short ratecard showing committed vs burst pricing. Lauren — I can draft that and attach a rough ratecard PDF. Marissa — can you confirm if we should include a short canary plan (1–2 endpoints, 2–3 day ramp) in the quote?

—Ben
Ben Carter
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com

Thanks Ben — that framing is super helpful and aligns with what Brightlane needs. Quick summary / agreed next steps so we can track: 

Agreed technical framing:
- Concurrency counts by active in-flight sessions (multiplexed streams each count).
- Recommend reserving for 250 concurrent sessions to cover steady-state + bursts.
- Baseline committed QPS: 120 with burst window to 350 for 1–5 minutes (Redwood will model the burst credit math).
- Streaming latency SLO target: first-byte 95th <250ms; tail token emission <300ms (we’ll validate with canary).

Immediate next steps:
1) Redwood to provide formal ratecard/quote (Hosted w/ burst credits option + Dedicated pool option) by EOD Friday. Attachments: redwood-ratecard-draft.pdf.
2) Schedule infra deep-dive next Tue (30–45m). Ben to invite Infra perf lead; Amira to invite an engineer who can run a small client test.
3) Lauren/Ben to include a one-page canary playbook in the proposal (1–2 endpoints, 48–72 hour ramp, sanity checks for latency and error rates).
4) Amira to confirm procurement timeline/end-of-month T&Cs window.

Amira — if you can send the session distribution CSV (peak vs baseline by hour) that’ll help be precise in GPU sizing. We’ll iterate quickly and get a quote over.

—Lauren
